prompt: An assistant "checks today's date". What does the model itself do?
hint: A model produces one kind of thing.

choices.text: It writes a request for the date tool
choices.why: Right. The program around it reads that line and runs the tool.

choices.text: It reads the computer's clock
choices.why: A model cannot reach a clock or anything else. It writes text.

choices.text: It remembers the date from its training
choices.why: That would be a likely date, not today's (lesson 5).

choices.text: It runs a small program it wrote
choices.why: It can write a program, as text. Running it is somebody else's job.

prompt: In `agent runs/order.txt`, who produced the lines starting `tool>`?
hint: Which lines come from the turn file?

choices.text: The course, which wrote them into the turn file
choices.why: The turn file holds only the model's side: the `Action:` and `Answer:` lines.

choices.text: The model, predicting what the tool would say
choices.why: `agent` never prints what a turn claims a tool said. It prints what the tool returned.

choices.text: A second language model that imitates each tool
choices.why: There is no second model. `today` and `calculator` are ordinary programs.

choices.text: Real tools, run by `agent`
choices.why: Yes. The `model>` lines are the turn file; the date and `127.5` were produced by the tools themselves.

prompt: Why give the model a calculator for `3 * 42.50` instead of letting it write the total?
hint: Lesson 3: how do digits reach a model?

choices.text: Models refuse to do arithmetic unless a tool is available
choices.why: They do arithmetic readily, and they sometimes get it wrong without any sign.

choices.text: The calculator is cheaper than any model call
choices.why: Cost is not the reason given. Correctness is.

choices.text: A computed result replaces a likely one
choices.why: Right. The model sees digits in chunks; the calculator gives the exact value every time.

choices.text: The model cannot read numbers that contain a decimal point
choices.why: It reads them; the trouble is lining digits up across chunks.

prompt: How does a model find out which tools it may ask for?
hint: Where does everything the model knows about this request come from?

choices.text: It discovers them by trying names until one works
choices.why: It can only use what it was told about; an unknown name gets an error.

choices.text: From its input
choices.why: Yes. A description in the prompt, or the API's field for tools. Each tool is described by a name, what it does and what input it takes.

choices.text: Every model is trained with the same fixed list of tools
choices.why: Tools differ by application. They are described in each request.

choices.text: The tools announce themselves to the model over the network
choices.why: Nothing reaches the model except the text of the request.

prompt: "The description is a prompt too." What follows for the sentence that describes a tool?
hint: How does the model decide whether and how to call it?

choices.text: Nothing, since the model ignores tool descriptions and reads only the name
choices.why: The description is often all the model has to go on.

choices.text: It steers whether and how the model calls the tool
choices.why: Right. Saying the calculator takes numbers and + - * / tells the model what input will work.

choices.text: It is checked by the provider, so its wording does not matter
choices.why: Nobody rewrites it for you. Its wording is part of what the model continues from.

choices.text: It runs the tool, so it has to be valid code
choices.why: The description is plain text for the model. The tool is code elsewhere.

prompt: What did the calculator return for `3 * 42.50` in the run?
In the live run of the cake order, which part of the answer came from no tool?

choices.text: Today's date, Friday 2 October 2026
choices.why: That came from `today`, on the one `tool>` line.

choices.text: The total, R$ 127.50
choices.why: Yes. The model asked for the calculator in the same turn as `today`, only the first request ran, and the total is its own arithmetic.

choices.text: Nothing; the answer copies the tools
choices.why: Only one tool ran, and the answer has more in it than a date.

choices.text: The name of the café, from search
choices.why: `search` was never asked for in this run.

prompt: In a turn file for `agent`, one turn is separated from the next by a line holding ___.
hint: Three characters, the same three each time.

prompt: What does this course mean by an agent?
hint: The last part of the first section.

choices.text: Any chat assistant
choices.why: A chat assistant with no tools is not one in this sense.

choices.text: A model that can act without any program around it
choices.why: Nothing acts without the program; the model only writes.

choices.text: A model looping through tool requests
choices.why: Right. The program runs the tools and holds the limits.

choices.text: A person who supervises a model
choices.why: The word here names the model in its loop, not a person.

prompt: The model asked for `weather[São Paulo]` and `agent` answered `error: there is no tool called weather`. Why is that better than returning nothing?
hint: What would the model do with silence?

choices.text: An error stops the run at once, which is always safest
choices.why: The run went on: the next turn answered honestly.

choices.text: The model reads the error and answers honestly
choices.why: Right. Silence or an empty result leaves room for a likely forecast.

choices.text: Errors cost no tokens
choices.why: The error is text and is counted like any other.

choices.text: It makes the model build a weather tool
choices.why: A model cannot build or run tools. It can only ask.

prompt: With `--allow calculator`, `today` was refused, and the answer still said "Saturday 3 October". Why?

choices.text: The turns were written in advance and played back regardless
choices.why: Right. A real model at step 3 would have no date in front of it; naming a day would be invented.

choices.text: The calculator worked out the date
choices.why: The calculator returned 127.5 and nothing else.

choices.text: The refusal message contained the date
choices.why: It said only that `today` was not allowed.

choices.text: `agent` retried `today` without telling anyone
choices.why: It refused the call; nothing ran.

hint: What did the `--allow calculator` run prevent, and what did it not?

choices.text: That the model's answer is correct
choices.why: The refused run still produced an answer naming a day it could not know.

choices.text: That the model will not ask for a forbidden tool
choices.why: It asked for `today` anyway. The refusal happened in the program.

choices.text: That the run will finish within the step limit
choices.why: Steps are limited by `--max-steps`, a separate check.

choices.text: What runs, not what is true
choices.why: Right. It controls actions. Truth still has to be checked another way.

prompt: `agent runs/unfinished.txt` ran out of turns before an `Answer:`. How many steps did it report?
Why does `agent` report a run that hits its limit as stopped rather than answered?

choices.text: Because a stopped run is cheaper
choices.why: Cost does not change what the run produced: no answer.

choices.text: Because the model asked it to
choices.why: The model has no say in how the loop reports.

choices.text: So whoever called it knows there is no answer
choices.why: Right. The caller then raises the limit, asks a person, or gives up honestly. Turning "no answer" into an answer would hide the failure.

choices.text: Because the last tool result counts as the answer
choices.why: A tool result is evidence for the model, not the reply.

prompt: Which of these are decided by the program running the loop? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Which tools exist
choices.why: Yes: `weather` did not, so nothing ran.

choices.text: Which tools this task may use
choices.why: Yes: `--allow` set it.

choices.text: How many turns the loop plays
choices.why: Yes: `--max-steps`.

choices.text: Which tool to ask for next
choices.why: That is the model's decision, written as an `Action:` line.

prompt: Why put "only use the calculator" in the program rather than only in the prompt?
hint: Lesson 7 is about the text that persuades a model.

choices.text: A check in the program holds whatever the model was persuaded of
choices.why: Right. A sentence in the prompt is a request; the program's check is a fact about what runs.

choices.text: Models ignore every instruction in a prompt
choices.why: They follow instructions often. The point is not depending on it.

choices.text: Prompts cannot mention tools
choices.why: Prompts describe tools all the time.

choices.text: The program runs faster than the model reads
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

prompt: Put one round of the loop in order.
hint: It starts with the model's text.
items: The model writes an Action line
The program checks the tool is allowed
The result goes into the text and the model is asked again

prompt: Match each way a run ended with what `agent` printed.
hint: The four runs of the second section.

pairs.left: a tool that does not exist
pairs.right: error: there is no tool called weather

pairs.left: a tool that is not allowed
pairs.right: refused: today is not allowed in this task
